title.value: On the Limitations of the Elo, Real-World Games are Transitive, not Additive
title.justification: The paper focuses on the limitations of the Elo scoring system and proposes a new decomposition for better ranking in terms of transitivity and cyclicity of real-world games.
title.quote: On the Limitations of the Elo, Real-World Games are Transitive, not Additive

extractions.description: This paper investigates the limitations of the Elo score system predominantly used in ranking players in competitive games, such as chess or StarCraft II, which assumes an additive nature. It introduces an alternative ranking method to properly extract transitive components in games. The proposed disc decomposition method is validated on real-world games, showing improved prediction performance over the traditional Elo score. It also provides a transitive and cyclic analysis within the game structures, using skew-symmetric matrix decomposition.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The central focus of the paper is on game theory, specifically related to ranking and predicting outcomes in competitive games. It does not directly address issues related to climate or ecological sustainable development.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: This paper investigates the challenge of identifying transitive components in games and proposes an alternative ranking system that properly extracts the transitive components in these games.

primary_category.justification: The paper's focus is on the mathematical and methodological aspects of game theory, dealing with ranking systems and game transitivity/cyclicity. It does not relate to climate or ecological sustainability directly.
primary_category.quote: The Elo score has been extensively used to rank players by their skill or strength in competitive games such as chess, go, or StarCraft II.

secondary_categories.quote: Accurately evaluating and ranking players in games has been a concern for decades.

primary_sub_category.quote: We propose a disc decomposition (Theorem 2) which yields a quantitative and tractable definition of the amount of transitivity of a real-world game.
